content: Haskins Laboratories is an independent, multidisciplinary research institute that focuses on the biological foundations of spoken and written language, including speech, language, and reading. It was founded in 1935 and has been located in New Haven, Connecticut, since 1970. The institute has a long history of groundbreaking contributions, such as developing the first rules for speech synthesis, creating a prototype reading machine for the blind, and introducing the concept of phonemic awareness as a critical skill for learning to read. 1930s Haskins Laboratories was established in 1935 by Caryl Haskins and Franklin S. Cooper. Initially affiliated with Harvard University, MIT, and Union College, the institute conducted research in microbiology, radiation physics, and other fields. In 1939, the Laboratories moved to New York City, where Seymour Hutner joined to develop research programs in microbiology, genetics, and nutrition. This program later evolved into a part of Pace University. 1940s During World War II, the U.S. Office of Scientific Research and Development tasked Haskins Laboratories with developing technologies to assist blinded veterans. Alvin Liberman, an experimental psychologist, worked on creating a sound alphabet for a reading machine for the blind. Luigi Provasoli established a marine biology research program, which later moved to Yale University in 1970 and ended with his retirement in 1978. 1950s Franklin S. Cooper invented the Pattern Playback, a device that converted visual representations of speech into sound. Using this tool, Cooper, Alvin Liberman, and Pierre Delattre identified the acoustic cues for perceiving phonetic segments like consonants and vowels. This work led to the development of the motor theory of speech perception, which proposed that speech perception relies on a biological specialization for understanding the acoustic consequences of articulation. Liberman and his team also created a set of rules for speech synthesis using the Pattern Playback. 1960s Franklin S. Cooper and Katherine Safford Harris introduced electromyographic techniques to study the neuromuscular organization of speech. Leigh Lisker and Arthur Abramson demonstrated that voice onset time (VOT) is a key factor in distinguishing voiced and voiceless consonants. Donald Shankweiler and Michael Studdert-Kennedy used dichotic listening experiments to show that phonetic perception is distinct from general auditory perception and is typically processed in the left hemisphere of the brain. Researchers also connected their first computer to a speech synthesizer, enabling the development of a program for synthesizing continuous speech from phonetically spelled input. 1970s Haskins Laboratories relocated to New Haven, Connecticut, and established affiliations with Yale University and the University of Connecticut. Researchers, including Isabelle Liberman, Donald Shankweiler, and Alvin Liberman, developed the concept of phonemic awareness, emphasizing its importance for reading. Patrick Nye led efforts to create a reading machine for the blind, culminating in the development of an automatic text-to-speech system. Philip Rubin advanced sinewave synthesis, demonstrating that speech could be perceived without traditional speech cues. Rubin and colleagues also developed the first articulatory synthesizer, which allowed for interactive experiments on speech production. 1980s Research at Haskins supported the hypothesis that reading activates the phonological form of a word before or alongside its meaning. Carol Fowler proposed the direct realism theory of speech perception, suggesting that listeners perceive speech gestures directly from the acoustic signal. J.A. Scott Kelso and colleagues demonstrated functional synergies in speech gestures, while Elliot Saltzman developed a dynamical systems model of speech production. Catherine Browman and Louis Goldstein introduced articulatory phonology, which views gestures as the fundamental units of both phonetic action and phonological knowledge. These models were integrated into a computational framework for studying speech production. 1990s Katherine Safford Harris and Frederica Bell-Berti investigated the timing and coordination of speech gestures. Kenneth Pugh pioneered the use of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to study brain activity related to reading and reading disabilities. Philip Rubin, Louis Goldstein, and Mark Tiede developed CASY (Configurable Articulatory Synthesizer), a 3D model of the vocal tract that replicated MRI images of speakers. Researchers also explored the relationship between speech production and perception, as well as the role of phonological deficits in reading disabilities. 2000s Anne Fowler and Susan Brady launched the Early Reading Success (ERS) program, which focused on improving reading instruction for young children through professional development for teachers. David Ostry and colleagues studied motor control using robotic systems to influence jaw movement. Douglas Whalen and Khalil Iskarous combined ultrasound and opto-electronic tracking to study speech articulators. Donald Shankweiler and David Braze developed an eye-tracking laboratory to investigate reading processes in typical and disabled readers. In 2005, Haskins Laboratories moved to a new, state-of-the-art facility in New Haven. Notable Researchers Key contributors to Haskins Laboratories' work include Franklin S. Cooper, Alvin Liberman, Isabelle Liberman, Philip Rubin, Carol Fowler, Louis Goldstein, and many others. Key Topics Haskins Laboratories has made significant contributions to areas such as phonemic awareness, speech synthesis, articulatory phonology, reading pedagogy, and the development of technologies like the reading machine for the blind. Their work has advanced understanding in fields like cognitive neuroscience, experimental psychology, and linguistics.
